nameStory: The Angulose Prominent gets its name from the angular, zigzag patterns on its forewings that create distinctive sharp-edged shapes. The word 'angulose' comes from the Latin 'angulus' meaning angle, referring to these geometric wing markings that help distinguish it from other prominent moths.
description: The Angulose Prominent is a medium-sized moth with a wingspan of about 1.5 inches that flies from late spring through summer. Like other prominent moths, it has a sturdy, somewhat chunky build with forewings that often display intricate patterns of browns, grays, and earth tones. When at rest, these moths typically hold their wings in a tent-like position over their body. The caterpillars feed exclusively on oak trees, making this species closely tied to oak forest habitats.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive angular, zigzag lines across the forewings that create sharp geometric patterns in shades of brown and gray

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized moth with wingspan of 35-45mm (about 1.5 inches), noticeably larger than many common house moths

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: Holds wings in a triangular tent shape over the body when at rest, creating a peaked roofline silhouette

idTips.label: Body Build
idTips.description: Robust, fuzzy body that feels substantial if gently handled, not delicate like many smaller moths

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Earth-toned wings in various shades of brown, gray, and sometimes buff, blending well with tree bark

habitat: Found in oak forests and woodlands throughout New England, from mixed hardwood forests at lower elevations to oak-dominated hillsides. Look for them near mature oak trees, especially white oak, red oak, and other Quercus species that serve as their caterpillar host plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May as oak leaves fully develop. Look for them at porch lights or tree trunks during warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period through August. Moths are most active at night and may be found resting on tree bark during the day.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity winds down by early fall. Eggs and early-stage caterpillars may be present on oak leaves.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae in the soil. No adult activity during cold months.

funFact: Despite being called 'prominent' moths, many species in this family get their name not from being easy to spot, but from the prominent tufts or humps that stick up from their caterpillars' backs, making the larvae look like tiny prehistoric monsters!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other prominent moths in the same family, but the angular zigzag wing patterns are distinctive. Memory trick: 'Angulose has angles' - look for those sharp, geometric lines rather than smooth curves or simple bands.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Prominent Moths' can be misleading since it refers to projections on the caterpillars, not the visibility of the adult moths. These moths are actually quite well-camouflaged and blend in with tree bark when resting during the day.
compareHints: As the only Peridea species commonly found in New England, compare it with other prominent moths like the White-dotted Prominent or Elegant Prominent. The Angulose Prominent's angular wing patterns are more geometric and sharp-edged compared to the softer, more flowing patterns of its relatives.
